claim: France was one of the most affected European countries by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020.
source: Although France was one of the most affected European countries by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, the dynamics of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) movement within France, but also involving France in Europe and in the world, remain only partially characterized in this timeframe.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a contextual statement about France's pandemic experience.

claim: The study analyzed 638,706 GISAID deposited sequences from January 1 to December 31, 2020.
source: Here, we analyzed GISAID deposited sequences from January 1 to December 31, 2020 (n = 638,706 sequences at the time of writing).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of sequences analyzed and the time period.

claim: The study produced 100 subsamples of sequences and related phylogenetic trees for different geographic scales and time periods.
source: To tackle the challenging number of sequences without the bias of analyzing a single subsample of sequences, we produced 100 subsamples of sequences and related phylogenetic trees from the whole dataset for different geographic scales (worldwide, European countries, and French administrative regions) and time periods (from January 1 to July 25, 2020, and from July 26 to December 31, 2020).
evidence: The methodology is explicitly described in the abstract.

claim: The study applied a maximum likelihood discrete trait phylogeographic method to date exchange events.
source: We applied a maximum likelihood discrete trait phylogeographic method to date exchange events (i.e., a transition from one location to another one), to estimate the geographic spread of SARS-CoV-2 transmissions and lineages into, from and within France, Europe, and the world.
evidence: The methodological approach is explicitly stated in the abstract.

claim: Two different patterns of exchange events were observed between the first and second half of 2020.
source: The results unraveled two different patterns of exchange events between the first and second half of 2020.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Europe was systematically associated with most of the intercontinental exchanges throughout 2020.
source: Throughout the year, Europe was systematically associated with most of the intercontinental exchanges.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 was mainly introduced into France from North America and Europe during the first European epidemic wave.
source: SARS-CoV-2 was mainly introduced into France from North America and Europe (mostly by Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, Belgium, and Germany) during the first European epidemic wave.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, Belgium, and Germany were the main European sources of SARS-CoV-2 introduction into France during the first wave.
source: SARS-CoV-2 was mainly introduced into France from North America and Europe (mostly by Italy, Spain, the United Kingdom, Belgium, and Germany) during the first European epidemic wave.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a finding.

claim: During the second wave, exchange events were limited to neighboring countries without strong intercontinental movement.
source: During the second wave, exchange events were limited to neighboring countries without strong intercontinental movement, but Russia widely exported the virus into Europe during the summer of 2020.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Russia widely exported the virus into Europe during the summer of 2020.
source: During the second wave, exchange events were limited to neighboring countries without strong intercontinental movement, but Russia widely exported the virus into Europe during the summer of 2020.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: France mostly exported B.1 lineage during the first European epidemic wave.
source: France mostly exported B.1 and B.1.160 lineages, respectively, during the first and second European epidemic waves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: France mostly exported B.1.160 lineage during the second European epidemic wave.
source: France mostly exported B.1 and B.1.160 lineages, respectively, during the first and second European epidemic waves.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: The Paris area was the main exporter during the first wave at the level of French administrative regions.
source: At the level of French administrative regions, the Paris area was the main exporter during the first wave.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: For the second epidemic wave, the Paris area and Lyon area equally contributed to virus spread.
source: But, for the second epidemic wave, it equally contributed to virus spread with Lyon area, the second most populated urban area after Paris in France.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Lyon area is the second most populated urban area after Paris in France.
source: But, for the second epidemic wave, it equally contributed to virus spread with Lyon area, the second most populated urban area after Paris in France.
evidence: This is stated as background information in the abstract.

claim: The main circulating lineages were similarly distributed among the French regions.
source: The main circulating lineages were similarly distributed among the French regions.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the abstract.

claim: An outbreak of severe respiratory disease was identified in Wuhan, China on December 1, 2019.
source: On December 1, 2019, an outbreak of severe respiratory disease was identified in the city of Wuhan, China (Huang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 was rapidly identified as the agent of the disease.
source: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) was rapidly identified as the agent of the disease (Zhu et al., 2020), responsible for the ongoing global pandemic of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: By the end of 2020, the virus caused over 1.8 million deaths worldwide.
source: By the end of 2020, the virus caused over 1.8 million deaths worldwide including ~65,000 deaths in France, concomitantly with social and economic devastations in many regions of the world (Mofijur et al., 2021; Santomauro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: By the end of 2020, approximately 65,000 deaths occurred in France.
source: By the end of 2020, the virus caused over 1.8 million deaths worldwide including ~65,000 deaths in France, concomitantly with social and economic devastations in many regions of the world (Mofijur et al., 2021; Santomauro et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Epidemiological models have been helpful to quantify viral spread and inform public health decisions.
source: Epidemiological models have been particularly helpful to quantify viral spread both in the short and long terms and to inform public health decisions (Hoertel et al., 2020; Kissler et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Viral whole-genome sequencing has become a powerful tool to better understand infection dynamics.
source: In addition to clinical and epidemiological insights, viral whole-genome sequencing has become a powerful and invaluable tool to better understand infection dynamics (Volz et al., 2013), including the COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: The number of available SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences has rapidly grown thanks to international networks such as GISAID.
source: The number of available SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences has rapidly grown thanks to the efforts of scientists and researchers gathered via international networks such as the Global Initiative on Sharing All Influenza Data, GISAID (https://www.gisaid.org/; Khare et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: Genomic data have become a strong asset to inform governments and help public health decisions.
source: Genomic data have become a strong asset in addition to epidemiological data to inform governments and help public health decisions (Attwood et al., 2022; Rife et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support it.

claim: Existing phylogenetic tools are limited for studying large amounts of data due to computational time required.
source: However, due to the computational time required for many analyses, existing phylogenetic tools are limited for studying large amounts of data such as those generated by widespread viral sequencing.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a methodological challenge.

claim: The first COVID-19 suspected case in France was identified in late December 2019.
source: In France, the first COVID-19 suspected case was identified in late December 2019 (Deslandes et al., 2020), and the first confirmed cases of SARS-CoV-2 infection were detected on January 24, 2020, in individuals who had recently traveled in China (Bernard Stoecklin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: The first confirmed cases of SARS-CoV-2 infection in France were detected on January 24, 2020, in individuals who had recently traveled in China.
source: In France, the first COVID-19 suspected case was identified in late December 2019 (Deslandes et al., 2020), and the first confirmed cases of SARS-CoV-2 infection were detected on January 24, 2020, in individuals who had recently traveled in China (Bernard Stoecklin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support it.

claim: COVID-19 cases remained scarce in France until the end of February 2020.
source: COVID-19 cases remained scarce until the end of February, when the national incidence curve of new SARS-CoV-2 infections started to rise (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Figure 1.

claim: A complete lockdown was implemented across France from March 17 to May 10, 2020.
source: By the end of February, reinforced measures were announced, including social distancing, cessation of passenger flights to France, school closure, and finally, a complete lockdown across the entire country from March 17 to May 10, 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a factual event.

claim: The reported daily incidence and numbers of severe cases peaked at the beginning of April 2020.
source: The reported daily incidence and numbers of severe cases peaked at the beginning of April 2020 before decreasing steadily until August 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation.

claim: A second wave of infections occurred in early September 2020 after the relaxation of social distancing measures in June.
source: However, after the relaxation of social distancing measures in June, a second wave of infections occurred in early September peaking at more than 100,000 positive cases and 1300 confirmed deaths in a single day on November 2, 2020 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Figure 1.

claim: The second wave peaked at more than 100,000 positive cases and 1300 confirmed deaths in a single day on November 2, 2020.
source: However, after the relaxation of social distancing measures in June, a second wave of infections occurred in early September peaking at more than 100,000 positive cases and 1300 confirmed deaths in a single day on November 2, 2020 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Figure 1.

claim: A second national lockdown was applied in France between October 29 and December 15, 2020.
source: After this peak, daily incidence and severe COVID-19 cases gradually diminished down to a number of positive daily cases varying between 2000 and 25,000 at the end of 2020 thanks to a second national lockdown applied between October 29 and December 15, 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a factual event.

claim: Epidemiological trends were similar in most European countries except for Russia or Romania.
source: Epidemiological trends were similar in most European countries except for Russia or Romania, where high rates of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths were reported even in the summer of 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation.

claim: High rates of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths were reported in Russia and Romania even in the summer of 2020.
source: Epidemiological trends were similar in most European countries except for Russia or Romania, where high rates of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths were reported even in the summer of 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an observation.

claim: The number of deaths increased about 2 weeks later in North America compared to Europe and remained high throughout 2020.
source: Of note, the other continents showed different patterns of virus circulation: compared to Europe, the number of deaths increased about 2 weeks later in North America and remained high throughout 2020; and from early May, Asia and South America were also highly impacted by the pandemic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: From early May 2020, Asia and South America were highly impacted by the pandemic.
source: Of note, the other continents showed different patterns of virus circulation: compared to Europe, the number of deaths increased about 2 weeks later in North America and remained high throughout 2020; and from early May, Asia and South America were also highly impacted by the pandemic (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A total of 638,706 sequences were retained in the study from January 1 to December 31, 2020.
source: From January 1 to December 31, 2020, a total of 638,706 sequences were retained in our study.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data point.

claim: The number of sequences for each country at each week was chosen to be proportional to the number of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths per country and per week with a 2-week shift.
source: The number of sequences for each country at each week was chosen to be proportional to the number of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths per country and per week with a 2-week shift to account for the time between infection and death.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological choice.

claim: Parameters were correctly estimated with limited variability across the 50 replicates in the simulation study.
source: Parameters were correctly estimated with limited variability across the 50 replicates.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing simulation results.

claim: The median parameters across replicates gave a very accurate estimation.
source: The median parameters across replicates gave a very accurate estimation (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2A.

claim: A slope of −0.7 was estimated for the relationship between log(error) and log(N) when evaluating error on parameter estimates across subsamples.
source: Using the relationship between log(error) as a function of log(N), we estimated a slope of −0.7 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Inferences conducted on subsamples of the same phylogenetic tree are partly independent.
source: Thus, inferences conducted on subsamples of the same phylogenetic tree are partly independent.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the simulation study.

claim: A mean error rate of 2.7% was found over the 100 subsamples when estimating the number of transitions.
source: We estimated the number of transitions (exchanges) of each type and compared them with the one obtained from the main tree, finding a mean error rate of 2.7% over the 100 subsamples (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Using subsamples of 1000 sequences from a large dataset and performing partially independent replicates is sufficient to accurately estimate transition events.
source: Altogether, these simulations suggested that using subsamples of 1000 sequences from a large dataset and performing partially independent replicates seems to be sufficient to accurately estimate transition events.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the simulation study.

claim: There was a positive correlation between the weekly number of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths and the weekly number of sequences included for a subsample.
source: For each geographic scale and time period, there was a positive correlation between the weekly number of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths and the weekly number of sequences we included for a subsample (Spearman's rank correlation, p < 0.001; r = 0.94 for the lowest correlation).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical support.

claim: A total of 39,288 distinct SARS-CoV-2 sequences were included across the 100 sampled phylogenies for the worldwide dataset for the first time period.
source: Overall, a total of 39,288 and 39,755 distinct SARS-CoV-2 sequences were included across the 100 sampled phylogenies for the worldwide dataset, respectively, for the first and the second time periods (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: A total of 39,755 distinct SARS-CoV-2 sequences were included across the 100 sampled phylogenies for the worldwide dataset for the second time period.
source: Overall, a total of 39,288 and 39,755 distinct SARS-CoV-2 sequences were included across the 100 sampled phylogenies for the worldwide dataset, respectively, for the first and the second time periods (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: At the European scale, 26,757 different SARS-CoV-2 sequences covering 11 countries were analyzed across the 100 subsamples for the first time period.
source: At the European scale, 26,757 and 27,658 different SARS-CoV-2 sequences covering 11 countries were analyzed across the 100 subsamples (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: At the European scale, 27,658 different SARS-CoV-2 sequences covering 11 countries were analyzed across the 100 subsamples for the second time period.
source: At the European scale, 26,757 and 27,658 different SARS-CoV-2 sequences covering 11 countries were analyzed across the 100 subsamples (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: PACA was the only French region that highly sequenced SARS-CoV-2 in 2020.
source: The Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur (PACA, Marseille area) was the only region that highly sequenced SARS-CoV-2 in 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation about sequencing efforts.

claim: 2543 unique sequences were considered across the 100 subsamples for French regions between January 1 and July 25, 2020.
source: We thus considered 2543 unique sequences across the 100 subsamples between January 1 and July 25, 2020, and 3124 unique sequences between July 26 and December 31, 2020 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: 3124 unique sequences were considered across the 100 subsamples for French regions between July 26 and December 31, 2020.
source: We thus considered 2543 unique sequences across the 100 subsamples between January 1 and July 25, 2020, and 3124 unique sequences between July 26 and December 31, 2020 (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Table 1.

claim: The genomic diversity of circulating SARS-CoV-2 in the different continents, countries, and French regions was found to be similar.
source: The genomic diversity of circulating SARS-CoV-2 in the different continents, countries, and French regions was found to be similar (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Genomes showed high sequence conservation compared to the Wuhan-Hu-1 reference in 2020 with a mean and median of approximately 13 SNPs.
source: Overall, genomes showed high sequence conservation compared to the Wuhan-Hu-1 reference in 2020 (mean and median of ~13 single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) with 95% of the distribution comprised between 4 and 25 SNPs).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: Europe (excluding France) accounted for 57.3% of the total number of exportation events between January 1 and July 25, 2020.
source: Between January 1 and July 25, 2020 (covering the first European epidemic wave), we found that Europe (excluding France) accounted for 57.3% of the total number of exportation events, and was the main source of SARS-CoV-2 exportations toward the other continents in all of the subsamples (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: North America participated in 24.3% of virus exportation during the first time period.
source: North America also highly participated in virus exportation during this period time (24.3%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: South America and Asia were each associated with 7.1% of the total number of exportation events during the first time period.
source: South America and Asia were each associated with 7.1% of the total number of exportation events, consistent with a later circulation of the virus in these continents (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: France contributed 4.2% of the total exportation events between January 1 and July 25, 2020.
source: France was estimated to have contributed 4.2% of the total exportation events, indicating that France was not the major European source of SARS-CoV-2 at the international level between January 1 and July 25, 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: France was not the major European source of SARS-CoV-2 at the international level between January 1 and July 25, 2020.
source: France was estimated to have contributed 4.2% of the total exportation events, indicating that France was not the major European source of SARS-CoV-2 at the international level between January 1 and July 25, 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data.

claim: Exportation events from France during the first period mostly consisted of the B.1 (80.2%), B.1.1 (6.1%), and B.1.356 (3.5%) lineages.
source: These events mostly consisted of the B.1 (80.2%), B.1.1 (6.1%), and B.1.356 (3.5%) lineages (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: North America received 28.5% of SARS-CoV-2 introduction events during the first time period.
source: North America received a large proportion of SARS-CoV-2 from other continents (28.5% of the introduction events), followed by South America (23.1%) and Europe (17.3%) (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: South America received 23.1% of SARS-CoV-2 introduction events during the first time period.
source: North America received a large proportion of SARS-CoV-2 from other continents (28.5% of the introduction events), followed by South America (23.1%) and Europe (17.3%) (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: Europe received 17.3% of SARS-CoV-2 introduction events during the first time period.
source: North America received a large proportion of SARS-CoV-2 from other continents (28.5% of the introduction events), followed by South America (23.1%) and Europe (17.3%) (Figure 3A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: An average of 11.7% of all SARS-CoV-2 introductions were into France during the first time period.
source: An average of 11.7% of all SARS-CoV-2 introductions were into France, and originated from North America (50.7%) and Europe (45.7%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introductions into France during the first period originated from North America (50.7%) and Europe (45.7%).
source: An average of 11.7% of all SARS-CoV-2 introductions were into France, and originated from North America (50.7%) and Europe (45.7%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introductions into France during the first period consisted of the B.1 (71.9%) and B.1.1 (18.2%) lineages.
source: These introductions consisted of the B.1 (71.9%) and B.1.1 (18.2%) lineages (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: The first introductions into France were detected at the beginning of February 2020.
source: The first introductions into France were detected at the beginning of February, and progressively increased to reach a peak just before the nationwide lockdown from March 17, 2020 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 introductions into France progressively increased to reach a peak just before the nationwide lockdown from March 17, 2020.
source: The first introductions into France were detected at the beginning of February, and progressively increased to reach a peak just before the nationwide lockdown from March 17, 2020 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Only South America and Asia were associated with a continuous increase in SARS-CoV-2 introductions after March 17, 2020.
source: Only South America and Asia were associated with a continuous increase in SARS-CoV-2 introductions after this date, probably because no such drastic measures were generalized there and the circulation of the virus remained limited in these regions.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation with a speculative explanation.

claim: 1.4 times fewer exchange events worldwide were observed during the second time period compared to the first half of 2020.
source: From July 26 to December 31, 2020 (second European epidemic wave), we observed 1.4 times fewer exchange events worldwide compared to the first half of 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: Europe was the main source of exchanges with 49.9% of the exportation events during the second time period.
source: Europe was, as between January 1 and July 25, 2020, the main source of exchanges with a total of 49.9% of the exportation events across subsamples, followed by North America (18.0%), Asia (14.1%), and South America (9.5%) (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: North America accounted for 18.0% of exportation events during the second time period.
source: Europe was, as between January 1 and July 25, 2020, the main source of exchanges with a total of 49.9% of the exportation events across subsamples, followed by North America (18.0%), Asia (14.1%), and South America (9.5%) (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: Asia accounted for 14.1% of exportation events during the second time period.
source: Europe was, as between January 1 and July 25, 2020, the main source of exchanges with a total of 49.9% of the exportation events across subsamples, followed by North America (18.0%), Asia (14.1%), and South America (9.5%) (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: South America accounted for 9.5% of exportation events during the second time period.
source: Europe was, as between January 1 and July 25, 2020, the main source of exchanges with a total of 49.9% of the exportation events across subsamples, followed by North America (18.0%), Asia (14.1%), and South America (9.5%) (Figure 3A–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3.

claim: Most exchange events occurred during the summer period (June to August 2020) during the second time period.
source: Most of the events occurred during the summer period (June to August 2020), corresponding to the summer holidays in most countries of the world.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an observation with contextual explanation.

claim: France accounted for 8.3% of the exportation events during the second time period.
source: France accounted for 8.3% of the exportation events, but they were almost exclusively oriented toward other European countries (89.9%) and overall detected from August to November 2020 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with the SARS-CoV-2 incidence in this period in France (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: 89.9% of France's exportation events during the second period were oriented toward other European countries.
source: France accounted for 8.3% of the exportation events, but they were almost exclusively oriented toward other European countries (89.9%) and overall detected from August to November 2020 (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2), consistent with the SARS-CoV-2 incidence in this period in France (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: The B.1.160 lineage accounted for almost all (97.9%) the exportation events from France during the second period.
source: The B.1.160 lineage accounted for almost all the exportation events from France (97.9%) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 introductions into France during the second period mostly originated from Europe (81.9%).
source: In a similar fashion, SARS-CoV-2 introductions into France mostly originated from Europe (81.9%) (Figure 3B) and were detected at a low rate from April 2020, then at a higher but always limited rate from June 2020, and at a strong level in September and October 2020 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 introductions into France during the second period consisted in majority of B.1.177 (28.0%), B.1.160 (24.7%), B.1 (17.7%), B.1.1 (10.0%), and B.1.258 (7.6%) lineages.
source: These SARS-CoV-2 introductions into France consisted in majority of B.1.177 (28.0%), B.1.160 (24.7%), B.1 (17.7%), B.1.1 (10.0%), and B.1.258 (7.6%) lineages (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 3E.

claim: Italy was the major contributor to virus exportation toward other European countries between January 1 and July 25, 2020, with 41.5% of the total number of exportation events.
source: By calculating the count of introduction and exportation events between January 1 and July 25, 2020 across the subsamples, we observed that Italy was the major contributor to virus exportation toward other European countries, with an average of 41.5% of the total number of exportation events.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: The United Kingdom, France, and Spain participated in 21.6%, 18.1%, and 11.8% of the total number of exportation events in Europe during the first period, respectively.
source: The United Kingdom, France, and Spain also highly participated in virus exportation, and consisted of 21.6, 18.1, and 11.8% of the total number of exportation events, respectively (Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4.

claim: The number of all exportation events decreased after the implementation of lockdowns in different European countries during the first period.
source: The number of all exportation events however decreased after the implementation of lockdowns in the different countries (with the first one occurring in Italy on March 9, 2020) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: The first lockdown in Europe occurred in Italy on March 9, 2020.
source: The number of all exportation events however decreased after the implementation of lockdowns in the different countries (with the first one occurring in Italy on March 9, 2020) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a factual event.

claim: France mostly exported SARS-CoV-2 toward Belgium (25.5%), Germany (21.0%), and the United Kingdom (20.4%) during the first period.
source: France mostly exported SARS-CoV-2 toward Belgium (25.5%), Germany (21.0%), and the United Kingdom (20.4%), and a little less toward Spain (10.1%) and the Netherlands (9.2%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: All exportation events from France during the first period occurred before the official lockdown in France (March 17, 2020).
source: All of these events occurred before the official lockdown in France (March 17, 2020) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and consisted of the B.1 (78.5%), B.1.1 (8.8%), and B.1.356 (6.9%) lineages (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: Exportation events from France during the first period consisted of the B.1 (78.5%), B.1.1 (8.8%), and B.1.356 (6.9%) lineages.
source: All of these events occurred before the official lockdown in France (March 17, 2020) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and consisted of the B.1 (78.5%), B.1.1 (8.8%), and B.1.356 (6.9%) lineages (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: The United Kingdom accounted for a quarter of the total number of introduction events in Europe during the first period.
source: For all introduction events, the proportions were more balanced: the United Kingdom accounted for a quarter of the total number of events, while Russia, Belgium, Germany, Italy, Spain, France, and the Netherlands represented between 6.5 and 11.9% of the total number of events (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4D.

claim: A high rate of introduction events into France was observed in February and March before the lockdown and originated mostly from Italy (44.3%), the United Kingdom (30.8%), and Spain (14.6%).
source: In France, a high rate of introduction events was observed in February and March before the lockdown and originated mostly from Italy (44.3%), the United Kingdom (30.8%), and Spain (14.6%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introductions into France during the first period consisted in majority of the B.1.1 (47.9%) and B.1 (35.4%) lineages.
source: These introductions consisted in majority of the B.1.1 (47.9%) and B.1 (35.4%) lineages (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: 1.3 times fewer exchanges were estimated in Europe during the second time period compared to the first half of 2020.
source: The second time period (from July 26 to December 31, 2020) showed a different pattern of exchanges. Here, we estimated 1.3 times fewer exchanges compared to the first half of 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: Russia accounted for most of the exportation events (27.6%) in Europe during the second time period.
source: Russia accounted for most of the exportation events (27.6%) (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4.

claim: Exportation events from Russia were estimated to occur during the spring and summer periods of the second time period.
source: These events were estimated to occur during the spring (after the relaxation of containment measures in most European countries) and the summer periods (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Spain (16.9%), France (14.0%), Germany (10.2%), Italy (7.9%), Poland (7.5%), and the United Kingdom (6.6%) highly participated in virus exportation during the second period.
source: Spain (16.9%), France (14.0%), Germany (10.2%), Italy (7.9%), Poland (7.5%), and the United Kingdom (6.6%) also highly participated in virus exportation (Figure 4A–D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4.

claim: Most exportation events in Europe during the second period were detected between August and October 2020.
source: Most of these events were detected between August and October 2020 (Figure 4C), and strongly decreased just before the second lockdown in most European countries (the first one occurring in Spain on October 9, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4C.

claim: The first second lockdown in Europe occurred in Spain on October 9, 2020.
source: Most of these events were detected between August and October 2020 (Figure 4C), and strongly decreased just before the second lockdown in most European countries (the first one occurring in Spain on October 9, 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a factual event.

claim: France mostly exported the virus toward Italy (22.2%), Germany (21.3%), and Belgium (19.1%) during the second period.
source: France mostly exported the virus toward Italy (22.2%), Germany (21.3%), and Belgium (19.1%) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and mostly the B.1.160 lineage (79.2%) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by figures.

claim: France mostly exported the B.1.160 lineage (79.2%) during the second period.
source: France mostly exported the virus toward Italy (22.2%), Germany (21.3%), and Belgium (19.1%) (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2), and mostly the B.1.160 lineage (79.2%) (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Germany accounted for 23.8% of the total number of introductions in Europe during the second period.
source: Focusing on introduction events, Germany accounted for 23.8% of the total number of introductions, followed by the United Kingdom (15.3%), Italy (15.1%), and France (9.8%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: The United Kingdom accounted for 15.3% of introduction events in Europe during the second period.
source: Focusing on introduction events, Germany accounted for 23.8% of the total number of introductions, followed by the United Kingdom (15.3%), Italy (15.1%), and France (9.8%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: Italy accounted for 15.1% of introduction events in Europe during the second period.
source: Focusing on introduction events, Germany accounted for 23.8% of the total number of introductions, followed by the United Kingdom (15.3%), Italy (15.1%), and France (9.8%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: Russia accounted for less than 0.1% of introduction events in Europe during the second period.
source: For the remaining European countries, the proportion of introduction events was comprised between 4.5 and 7.6%, except for Russia that accounted for <0.1% of the events.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: Introductions into France during the second period mostly originated from Russia (31.7%) during the summer period.
source: Introductions into France mostly originated from Russia (31.7%) during the summer period, and later from Spain (23.7%), Italy (12.5%), and Germany (11.0%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Introductions into France during the second period later originated from Spain (23.7%), Italy (12.5%), and Germany (11.0%).
source: Introductions into France mostly originated from Russia (31.7%) during the summer period, and later from Spain (23.7%), Italy (12.5%), and Germany (11.0%) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 introductions into France during the second period consisted in majority of B.1.177 (31.0%), B.1.1 (22.6%) and B.1.258 (7.6%) lineages.
source: These SARS-CoV-2 introductions into France consisted in majority of B.1.177 (31.0%), B.1.1 (22.6%) and B.1.258 (7.6%) lineages (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: Only five French regions (ARA, BRE, IDF, OCC, and PACA) were investigated in the study.
source: As previously explained, only five regions (ARA, BRE, IDF, OCC, and PACA, which cover the most densely populated urban areas in France, that is, Paris, Lyon, Montpellier, Toulouse, and Marseille) were investigated since only a few, if any, sequences were available on GISAID for the other regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a methodological limitation.

claim: The Grand-Est region was one of the first massively affected by SARS-CoV-2 in France during the first wave.
source: Of note, the Grand-Est region was one of the first massively affected by SARS-CoV-2 in France during the first wave and, thus, must have played a major role.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as contextual information.

claim: The Grand-Est region not being sampled is a limitation of the study.
source: The fact that it was not sampled is a limitation that must be taken into account when reading these results.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an acknowledgment of a limitation.

claim: Almost all exportation events from French regions during the first wave originated from IDF (84.0%).
source: During the first French epidemic wave, almost all exportation events originated from IDF (84.0%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: ARA, BRE, OCC, and PACA accounted for 8.2%, 0.4%, 2.3%, and 5.1% of the total number of exportation events from French regions during the first wave, respectively.
source: ARA, BRE, OCC, and PACA only accounted for 8.2, 0.4, 2.3, and 5.1% of the total number of exportation events (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5.

claim: Most exportation events from French regions during the first wave occurred between February and March and largely decreased after the national lockdown.
source: As for the wider geographic scales, most exportation events occurred between February and March, and largely decreased after the national lockdown (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5.

claim: ARA was the region having most SARS-CoV-2 introductions during the first wave, with 48.3% of the total number of introduction events.
source: ARA was the region having most SARS-CoV-2 introductions, with 48.3% of the total number of introduction events, followed by PACA (22.1%), OCC (17.3%), and BRE (7.0%) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: PACA received 22.1% of introduction events among French regions during the first wave.
source: ARA was the region having most SARS-CoV-2 introductions, with 48.3% of the total number of introduction events, followed by PACA (22.1%), OCC (17.3%), and BRE (7.0%) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: All French regions were mostly affected by the B.1 lineage at similar rates during the first wave, except for OCC with more B.1.1 lineage.
source: All the regions were mostly affected by the B.1 lineage at similar rates, except for OCC with more B.1.1 lineage (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5E.

claim: IDF was no longer the single epicenter of SARS-CoV-2 inter-region exchanges during the second wave.
source: During the second wave, IDF was no longer the single epicenter of SARS-CoV-2 inter-region exchanges.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a key finding.

claim: Both IDF and ARA participated concomitantly in virus spread at similarly large levels during the second wave (43.3% and 42.6% of the total number of exportation events, respectively).
source: Both IDF and ARA participated concomitantly in virus spread at similarly large levels (43.3 and 42.6% of the total number of exportation events, respectively) (Figure 5A, B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5.

claim: The first exportation events from French regions during the second wave mostly occurred in the spring and summer in IDF.
source: The first exportation events mostly occurred in the spring and summer in IDF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: ARA was associated with a high increase in exportation events by the end of July during the second wave.
source: ARA was associated with a high increase in exportation events by the end of July, consistent with the resumption of the epidemic.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation with contextual explanation.

claim: The second national lockdown implemented on October 29, 2020 was associated with a strong decline of the number of exchange events among French regions.
source: Again, the second national lockdown – implemented in October 29, 2020 – was associated with a strong decline of the number of exchange events (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5D.

claim: PACA received 31.3% of the total number of introductions among French regions during the second wave.
source: Regarding introduction events, PACA received 31.3% of the total number of introductions, followed by ARA (24.7%), IDF (24.1%), OCC (11.5%), and BRE (8.2%).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: ARA, BRE, OCC, and PACA mostly sent and received the B.1.160 lineage during the second wave.
source: Overall, ARA, BRE, OCC, and PACA mostly sent and received the B.1.160 lineage.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a data observation.

claim: IDF showed a different pattern during the second wave, exporting at similar rates both the B.1.160 and the B.1.177 lineages.
source: Only IDF showed a different pattern, exporting at similar rates both the B.1.160 and the B.1.177 lineages (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Figure 5F.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 exchange events within France showed two distinct patterns between the first and second epidemic waves of 2020.
source: Altogether, SARS-CoV-2 exchange events within France showed two distinct patterns between the first and second epidemic waves of 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary conclusion.

claim: Most SARS-CoV-2 exchanges involved the Paris area during the first half of 2020.
source: While most SARS-CoV-2 exchanges involved the Paris area during the first half of 2020, the situation was much more balanced after the summer 2020 with the Lyon area (ARA) also contributing to many exchanges.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary conclusion.

claim: The situation was much more balanced after summer 2020 with the Lyon area (ARA) also contributing to many exchanges.
source: While most SARS-CoV-2 exchanges involved the Paris area during the first half of 2020, the situation was much more balanced after the summer 2020 with the Lyon area (ARA) also contributing to many exchanges.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a summary conclusion.

claim: Viral spread across French regions in summer 2020 could be explained by travel associated with the summer holidays.
source: Viral spread across French regions in summer 2020 could be explained by travel associated with the summer holidays.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a speculative explanation.

claim: Three studies have explored the virus spread in France but only focused on the first French epidemic wave.
source: To our knowledge, three studies have explored the virus spread in France, but only focused on the first French epidemic wave and/or could not address SARS-CoV-2 introduction events from other continents or other European countries (Danesh et al., 2020; Elie and Alizon, 2020; Gámbaro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support it.

claim: Other studies have focused on larger scales such as Europe as a whole but did not explore in-depth the dynamics of exchanges especially in France.
source: Other studies have focused on larger scales such as Europe as a whole, but did not explore in-depth the dynamics of exchanges especially in France (Hodcroft et al., 2021; Lemey et al., 2021; Nadeau et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support it.

claim: Most phylodynamics studies on SARS-CoV-2 are based on Bayesian approaches.
source: Methodologically, most phylodynamics studies on SARS-CoV-2, as well as on other viruses or pathogens, are based on Bayesian approaches (notably with the popular and robust BEAST tool; Drummond and Rambaut, 2007) using one or more phylogenetic trees composed of several thousand sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support it.

claim: Bayesian methods require high computational power, representing their main limitation.
source: To reconstruct the evolution parameters and ancestral states at nodes (here, the geographical area and the SARS-CoV-2 lineage), Bayesian methods require high computational power, representing their main limitation (Drummond and Rambaut, 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support it.

claim: Bayesian phylogenetic analysis on about 2800 SARS-CoV-2 sequences required over 150 hr to obtain enough samples from the posterior distribution.
source: As stated by Dellicour et al., Bayesian phylogenetic analysis on about 2800 SARS-CoV-2 sequences required over 150 hr to obtain enough samples from the posterior distribution across 15 parallel runs with a GPU accelerated implementation (Dellicour et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support it.

claim: The GISAID database stores 638,704 SARS-CoV-2 sequences for the year 2020 alone as of May 8, 2022.
source: Since the GISAID database stores several hundred thousand SARS-CoV-2 sequences (n = 638,704 on May 8, 2022 for the year 2020 alone), we believe that using a phylogeny of a few thousand sequences only might not be the best way to accurately infer exchange events.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a data point.

claim: Bayesian approach seems not to be more accurate than maximum likelihood for the reconstruction of ancestral states.
source: Bayesian approach seems not to be more accurate than maximum likelihood for the reconstruction of ancestral states (Hanson-Smith et al., 2010), and we gain a lot in terms of sampling, computational time, and trends by sampling 100 semi-independent subsamples.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support it.

claim: The maximum likelihood-based method was recently used to depict with accuracy the genomic epidemiology of the virus in Canada.
source: The maximum likelihood-based method was recently used to depict with accuracy the genomic epidemiology of the virus in Canada (McLaughlin et al., 2022), as well as in other contexts (Cunningham et al., 1998; Pupko et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to support it.

claim: France mostly exchanged SARS-CoV-2 with Europe and North America between January 1 and July 25, 2020.
source: Between January 1 and July 25, 2020 (first European epidemic wave), France mostly exchanged SARS-CoV-2 with Europe and North America.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: During the second European epidemic wave, France almost exclusively exchanged the virus with other European countries.
source: The observation contrasts with the second European epidemic wave – that took place between late October and the end of 2020 – where France almost exclusively exchanged the virus with other European countries.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The borders of France have gradually reopened with European countries but remained mostly closed to the rest of the world during the second wave.
source: This result is logical insofar as the borders of France have gradually reopened with European countries but remained mostly closed to the rest of the world.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an explanation for the findings.

claim: A very low rate of SARS-CoV-2 exchanges between Europe (including France) and Asia or South America was found in 2020.
source: A very low rate of SARS-CoV-2 exchanges between Europe (including France) and Asia or South America was found in 2020, which is not surprising since the virus started to spread in these continents only from May 2020 where all borders of Europe were already closed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings with explanation.

claim: France was a major source of SARS-CoV-2 exchange on the European scale.
source: On the European scale, France was a major source of SARS-CoV-2 exchange.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: France ranked third regarding exportation events in Europe between January 1 and July 25, 2020, only behind the United Kingdom and Italy.
source: It ranked third regarding exportation events (mainly directed toward neighboring countries) only behind the United Kingdom and Italy between January 1 and July 25, 2020, and third again behind Spain and Russia (where exchange events happened mostly in summer 2020) between July 26 and December 31, 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: France ranked third regarding exportation events in Europe between July 26 and December 31, 2020, behind Spain and Russia.
source: It ranked third regarding exportation events (mainly directed toward neighboring countries) only behind the United Kingdom and Italy between January 1 and July 25, 2020, and third again behind Spain and Russia (where exchange events happened mostly in summer 2020) between July 26 and December 31, 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The first cases introduced from European countries into France came from Italy and Spain.
source: The first cases introduced from European countries into France came from Italy and Spain, consistent with the early days of SARS-CoV-2 spread in Europe.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: These results are in line with the observations made across Europe through Bayesian inference.
source: These results are in line with the observations made across Europe through Bayesian inference (Lemey et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with a citation to support it.

claim: Both B.1 and B.1.1 were the most representative lineages introduced into or exported from France during the first wave.
source: In line with the lack of SARS-CoV-2 genomic diversity at the beginning of the pandemic, both B.1 and B.1.1 were the most representative lineages introduced into or exported from France.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Some cases were introduced into France from Russia during the second European epidemic wave where virus incidence was high since the summer 2020.
source: During the second European epidemic wave, some cases were introduced into France (and some other European countries) from Russia where virus incidence was high since the summer 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Most introductions into France during the second wave originated from Spain which initiated the second wave in European Union.
source: Then, most introductions into France originated from Spain which initiated the second wave in European Union, followed by Italy and Germany.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: Most of the introductions into France during the second wave were the lineages B.1.1, B.1.177, and B.1.258 that highly circulated in Europe.
source: Most of the introductions into France were the lineages B.1.1, B.1.177, and B.1.258 that highly circulated in Europe.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: France mostly exported the B.1.160 lineage during the second wave which was firstly detected in July 2020 in Marseille (PACA, France).
source: By contrast, France mostly exported the B.1.160 lineage which was firstly detected in July 2020 in Marseille (PACA, France), and represented the majority of sequences in fall 2020.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The frequency of the B.1.160 lineage decreased rapidly at the beginning of 2021 in favor of B.1.1.7.
source: The frequency of the B.1.160 lineage then decreased rapidly at the beginning of 2021 in favor of B.1.1.7.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an observation.

claim: The number of international exchanges was lower during the second wave compared to the first one.
source: Interestingly, the number of international exchanges was lower during the second wave compared to the first one, indicating the effectiveness of border control measures and that French people reduced travel outside France after the first national lockdown.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings with interpretation.

claim: The North and East of France (regions Hauts-de-France and Grand-Est) were not investigated in the study.
source: In addition to a limited overall size, genomic data only covered 5 out of 13 administrative regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). The North and East of France (i.e., regions Hauts-de-France and Grand-Est, respectively) that border Belgium, Luxembourg, and Germany, were not investigated.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a limitation.

claim: The evangelical gathering of the Christian Open-Door Church in Mulhouse took place from February 17 to 21, 2020 and consisted of approximately a thousand infected individuals.
source: More importantly, the region Grand-Est was associated with early large clusters that participated in virus spread across the country during the first European epidemic wave, such as the evangelical gathering of the Christian Open-Door Church (Mulhouse, Haut-Rhin) that took place from 17 to February 21, 2020 and consisted of approximately a thousand infected individuals.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as contextual information.

claim: Most of the exportations from French regions during the first wave originated from IDF (Paris area).
source: During the first wave, most of the exportations originated from IDF (Paris area).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The larger number of individuals living in IDF who left to other French regions at the beginning of the epidemic may be linked with most exportations originating from IDF during the first wave.
source: This may be linked with the larger number of individuals living in IDF who left to other French regions at the beginning of the epidemic.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculative explanation.

claim: A similar contribution of IDF to exchanges was observed during the second epidemic wave, but this time accompanied with ARA (Lyon area).
source: In the second epidemic wave, we observed a similar contribution of IDF to exchanges, but this time accompanied with ARA (Lyon area) which was associated with a strong SARS-CoV-2 incidence.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The circulation of lineages was the same between the French regions during both the first and second epidemic waves.
source: The circulation of lineages was the same between the French regions, both during the first and second epidemic waves.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: The B.1 was the major circulating lineage in French regions during the first wave.
source: The B.1 was the major circulating lineage during the first wave, while B.1.160 was mostly transmitted during the second one, concomitantly with B.1.177 in IDF.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: B.1.160 was mostly transmitted during the second wave in French regions, concomitantly with B.1.177 in IDF.
source: The B.1 was the major circulating lineage during the first wave, while B.1.160 was mostly transmitted during the second one, concomitantly with B.1.177 in IDF.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of findings.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences were downloaded from the GISAID database on May 8, 2022 (n = 10,005,024).
source: SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences were downloaded from the GISAID database on May 8, 2022 (n = 10,005,024).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a data point.

claim: Only complete viral genomes from infected individuals (more than 29 kb in length) were included in the study.
source: The following inclusion and exclusion criteria were applied to select samples for analysis: (1) only complete viral genomes from infected individuals (more than 29 kb in length) were included
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an inclusion criterion.

claim: The maximal proportion of undetermined nucleotide bases was fixed to 5% in the study.
source: (2) the maximal proportion of undetermined nucleotide bases was fixed to 5%;
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an inclusion criterion.

claim: Sequences with unknown or incomplete sampling dates, or unknown geographical location, were excluded from the study.
source: (3) sequences with unknown or incomplete sampling dates, or unknown geographical location, were excluded;
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an exclusion criterion.

claim: Sampling dates were comprised between January 1, 2020 and December 31, 2020 in the study.
source: (4) sampling dates were comprised between January 1, 2020 and December 31, 2020;
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an inclusion criterion.

claim: Sequences from non-human were excluded from the study.
source: and (5) sequences from non-human were excluded.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an exclusion criterion.

claim: The final dataset included 638,704 sequences after applying inclusion and exclusion criteria.
source: The final dataset included 638,704 sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a data point.

claim: 26,103 genomes were considered as outliers as they were in the extreme 5% regarding the number of non-synonymous mutations.
source: In a second pass, 26,103 genomes were considered as outliers as they were in the extreme 5% regarding the number of non-synonymous mutations.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a data processing step.

claim: The study used the number of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths per territory and per week as a proxy for virus circulation taking place 2 weeks earlier.
source: To determine the number of SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences to be included so as to be representative of each location epidemic, we used the number of SARS-CoV-2-related deaths per territory and per week as a proxy for virus circulation taking place 2 weeks earlier.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological choice.

claim: The study did not use SARS-CoV-2 detected cases as the proxy for infections because the intensity of COVID-19 testing was increased after the first wave.
source: We did not use SARS-CoV-2 detected cases as the proxy for infections because the intensity of COVID-19 testing was increased after the first wave, which probably increased the ascertainment probability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological justification.

claim: For the European scale, countries with more than 10,000 sequences were selected.
source: For the European scale, we selected countries with more than 10,000 sequences.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a selection criterion.

claim: Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Hungary were excluded despite passing the 10,000 sequences threshold for having too many weeks without enough data.
source: Ukraine, Czech Republic, and Hungary passed this threshold, but were excluded for having too many weeks without enough data.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an exclusion criterion.

claim: At the French region scale, only regions with less than 20% of weeks lacking data were included.
source: At the French region scale, we included only regions with less than 20% of weeks lacking data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as an inclusion criterion.

claim: Genome sequences were independently aligned against the Wuhan-Hu-1 reference genome using MAFFT v7.450.
source: For each subsample, genome sequences were independently aligned against the Wuhan-Hu-1 reference genome (GenBank accession: NC_045512.2) using MAFFT v7.450 then merged altogether (Katoh and Standley, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological step.

claim: The alignments were masked for problematic sites listed by Nicola De Maio et al.
source: The alignments were then masked for problematic sites listed by Nicola De Maio et al. (https://virological.org/t/masking-strategies-for-sars-cov-2-alignments/480).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological step with a citation.

claim: A maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree was inferred using FastTree v.2.1.11 under a GTR model.
source: From each masked alignment, we inferred a maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree using FastTree v.2.1.11 under a general time-reversible (GTR) model with a discrete gamma distribution to model inter-site rate variation and 1000 ultrafast-bootstraps to compute support values (Price et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological step with a citation.

claim: Each phylogenetic tree was dated using LSD2 v2.3 using Wuhan Hu-1 as outgroup for rooting.
source: Each phylogenetic tree was dated using LSD2 v2.3 using Wuhan Hu-1 as outgroup for rooting (To et al., 2016), with the parameter '-e 2' to be more stringent about outlier nodes.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological step with a citation.

claim: Ancestral state reconstructions of discrete geographical and SARS-CoV-2 lineage data were performed with the ace function of ape package in R.
source: For each phylogenetic tree we produced, ancestral state reconstructions of discrete geographical and SARS-CoV-2 lineage data were performed with the ace function of ape package in R (Paradis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological step with a citation.

claim: Three distinct Markov models of discrete character evolution through maximum likelihood were tested: ER, ARD, and SYM.
source: Three distinct Markov models of discrete character evolution through maximum likelihood were tested and compared: the Equal Rates (ER) which assumes a single rate of transition among all possible states, the All Rates Different (ARD) which allows a distinct rate for each position transition between two states, and the Symmetrical Rates (SYM) where forward and reverse transitions share the same parameter.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological approach.

claim: The study only presents results obtained with the SYM model because both the ARD and ER models led to nearly identical observations.
source: In this study, we only present the results obtained with the SYM model because both the ARD and ER models led to nearly identical observations compared to the SYM model.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section as a methodological justification.

claim: Nodes were assigned to a location when supported by ≥50% of the state likelihood.
source: From the ancestral state reconstruction, we assigned nodes to a location when supported by ≥50% of the state likelihood.
